common_name: Fedora 17 Hemp (Dual-Purpose Fiber and Grain Cultivar)

planting.note: Direct sow at or just after last frost into a dense, well-prepared seedbed; 'Fedora 17' is a French-bred, monoecious, day-neutral cultivar developed for combined fiber and grain harvest and requires state or federal licensing to grow in the United States.

directions: Drill seed about 3/4 inch deep at a dense rate to encourage tall, straight stalks with reduced branching, since crowding improves both fiber quality and lodging resistance; 'Fedora 17' is one of the most widely certified industrial hemp cultivars in Europe and appears on many US state-approved variety lists because its THC content reliably stays under the 0.3% compliance threshold. Being monoecious, every plant in the stand can be left to mature and set seed, simplifying dual-purpose harvest compared with dioecious cultivars that separate male and female plants. Cut stalks for fiber once flowering finishes and the lower leaves begin to yellow, or wait longer for the grain harvest if seed is the primary goal, though delaying reduces fiber quality as stems coarsen. A license from the appropriate state hemp program or the USDA is required before planting, and growers must submit to pre-harvest THC testing in most jurisdictions.
sources: European Union Common Catalogue of Varieties of Agricultural Plant Species
Kentucky Department of Agriculture Industrial Hemp Research Program

planting.note: Direct sow at or just after last frost into a dense stand; 'Futura 75' is a tall, late-maturing, monoecious French fiber cultivar and, like all hemp, requires state or federal licensing to grow legally in the United States.

directions: Drill seed at a high density of roughly 25-30 lb per acre to force tall, slender, largely unbranched stalks, since crowded stands are essential to good fiber quality in this cultivar. 'Futura 75' was bred in France for bast fiber production and has been used in several US university trials, including early Kentucky industrial hemp research plots, as a benchmark fiber-type cultivar because of its reliable low-THC compliance and strong stalk yield. Plants can reach 10 to 13 feet in a full season under good conditions, considerably taller than dual-purpose or grain cultivars, and stems become increasingly coarse and woody as flowering finishes. Harvest for fiber at the onset of flowering, when bast fiber content and quality peak, then ret and process the stalks as with any bast fiber crop; a hemp growing license and pre-harvest THC testing are required in nearly all US jurisdictions.
sources: European Union Common Catalogue of Varieties of Agricultural Plant Species

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed well past last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nankeen is a naturally tan-to-brown-lint heirloom selection of upland cotton requiring the same long, hot, frost-free season as any cotton.

directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm, following the same culture as any upland cotton. Nankeen is one of the oldest documented naturally colored cotton types, its warm tan-to-brown lint historically spun and woven into the durable buff-colored cloth that gave Nanjing, China's export cotton -- and eventually the color name "nankeen" -- its fame; Thomas Jefferson is recorded growing nankeen cotton in his Monticello gardens in the early 1800s. The lint's natural color eliminates the need for dyeing and tends to darken slightly with washing and UV exposure over the life of the finished cloth. Showy pale yellow flowers fade to pink before dropping to reveal green bolls that split open at full maturity, exposing the naturally tan lint; pick promptly once open to keep it clean and free of weathering stains. Rotate the planting site yearly and watch for the same boll weevil and aphid pressures as other cotton.
sources: Thomas Jefferson's Monticello -- Historic Vegetable and Fiber Varieties

common_name: Erlene's Green Cotton (Heirloom Naturally Green Cotton)

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed well past last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Erlene's Green is a naturally green-lint heirloom selection of upland cotton and needs the same long, hot, frost-free season as any cotton.

directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm, following standard upland cotton culture. Erlene's Green is a Southern heirloom naturally colored cotton, maintained and passed down by home seed savers, that produces sage-green lint instead of the usual white -- part of the same tradition of naturally pigmented cottons that inspired the modern Foxfibre breeding work reviving colored cotton for eco-conscious textile spinning. Pale yellow, hibiscus-like flowers fade to pink before dropping, and bolls split open at maturity to reveal soft green fiber that is prized by hand-spinners and fiber artists for producing yarn and cloth that needs no dye. Pick bolls promptly once open, since color and fiber quality can both fade with prolonged weather exposure, and rotate the planting site yearly to limit soil-borne disease buildup as with any cotton.
